title: Chewing mastic gum
summary: What Chios mastic resin is, how intentional chewing differs from soft modern diets and candy gum, oral-research angles, and how this app logs the habit.

sections.heading: What mastic gum actually is
sections.body: Mastic (often labeled Chios mastic) is the dried resin (tears) of the evergreen shrub Pistacia lentiscus, traditionally harvested on the Greek island of Chios. You chew the raw resin or commercial “mastic gum” pieces made from it—not bubble gum with synthetic rubber and sweeteners. Authentic mastic starts hard, softens with saliva and heat, stays firm for a long chew, and has a piney, slightly bitter aromatic flavor. That firmness is the practical point: it demands more sustained jaw work than soft commercial gum. Quality products list mastic resin (Pistacia lentiscus) as the base; cheap “mastic-flavored” candy gums are not the same material.

sections.heading: Mastication load in a soft-food world
sections.body: Human jaws and chewing muscles evolved under diets that required long, forceful mastication. Modern ultra-processed soft diets shorten chewing time and lower peak bite force for many people. Jaw elevators are still skeletal muscle—underuse deconditions them. Intentional hard chewing is one voluntary way to load those muscles—similar in spirit to resistance training, not magic. Realistic expectations: awareness of jaw use, possible endurance/tone with progressive practice, and a structured alternative to mindless snacking—not overnight facial bone remodeling.

sections.heading: Why people choose mastic over candy gum
sections.body: Sugar-free commercial gums can still be ultra-soft and easy to chew for hours with little resistance. Mastic’s higher chew resistance makes short sessions (often 10–20 minutes) feel like work. Lifestyle communities treat a daily mastic session as a discrete “jaw workout” plus an oral ritual that replaces grazing. That is behavioral design more than pharmacology: make the healthy default obvious and slightly effortful.

sections.heading: Oral research angles and TMJ safety
sections.body: Mastic resin has been studied for antimicrobial and oral-ecology properties; results vary by preparation and study quality. None of that turns recreational chewing into treatment for gum disease or ulcers—see a clinician for diagnosis. Chewing increases saliva flow if technique is clean (mostly nasal breathing, less air swallowing). Start 5–10 minutes if new to hard resin; chew evenly; stop for joint pain, ear pain, or tooth sensitivity. Clear hard mastic with a dentist if you have braces, recent dental work, active jaw pain, or night grinding.

sections.heading: Where Dr. Jack Kruse’s teaching is specific
sections.body: Kruse’s public material emphasizes real-food mastication and rejecting soft processed diets inside a broader ancestral-input and light–water–magnetism stack—not a single “gum protocol.” Product-level enthusiasm for Chios mastic and extreme facial-change claims are mostly community culture on top of ordinary muscle-use ideas. This app does not measure bite force or craniofacial growth.

sections.heading: What is solid, what is framework
sections.body: Solid ground: hard chewing loads jaw muscle; soft diets reduce mastication demand; saliva flow aids oral clearance. Framework: mastic as disease therapy, guaranteed bone remodeling, or a required mitochondrial keystone equal to light and sleep. Use it as optional Support jaw work beside real meals that still require chewing.

sections.heading: How to use it here
sections.body: Log Chewing mastic gum for real mastic resin/gum sessions (not candy gum). Duration can scale points within the cap. Equipment required—leave it off your available list if you do not own mastic. Pair with seafood-forward, less ultra-processed meals rather than using gum as the only mechanical load. Educational only.
